2935.tone: Source (Chaudhuri 2017, sec. 3.6): Bongcher is a contour tone language 'opposed to stress language'; two-way contrast, falling [grave] vs rising [acute], marked on the vowel; minimal pairs lùŋ 'heart' / lúŋ 'stone', nì 'day' / ní 'sun', ìn 'house' / ín 'drink', rìŋ 'neck' / ríŋ 'green', làm 'dance' / lám 'road', kòŋ 'waist' / kóŋ 'burn', rò 'rain' / ró 'bamboo', sàk 'sing' / sák 'eat', là 'take' / lá 'song', rùk 'steal' / rúk 'cover', nà 'pain' / ná 'place'. The word 'stress' occurs in ch.3 only in that typological contrast; 'prominence' occurs only for falling diphthongs (first element more prominent than the second), a diphthong-internal remark, not word stress. Other Halam varieties in the files: Debbarma 2017 Korbong ch.3 sec. 3.2 p.13 'Korbong is also a tone language where a change in the pitch of a syllable transforms a change in its meaning. Korbong has two lexical tones' (high, low); Debbarma 2018 Hrangkhawl ch.3 'Hrangkhawl shows two way tone contrast' and 'the analysis of tones is not extensive'; Kharlukhi 2012 ch.5 p.37 (Ranglong-Halam) 'only in Mara and Monsang tone is phonemic; while Halam and Biate do not have tone'. All are silent on word stress; the intra-Halam disagreement is about tone, not stress.

2946.dloc: Lapucci (ed.) 1986 §III 'Accenti' p. 17; Michelotti 2008 p. 204; Vitali 2008 §2.1 p. 13.
2946.heavy: Not a weight-to-stress system. The sources state the converse (stress-to-weight): Michelotti §2.2.1.3 'the syllable bearing primary stress contain two morae' (open syllable with long vowel or closed syllable with short vowel); Vitali 2008 §2.1 p. 13 and Vitali & Pioggia 2010 p. 4: /a i u/ and the long/open-mid vowels are long or occur only under stress. Epenthetic C-final paroxytones (fóran, védar, sàbet) show a closed final syllable can be unstressed, so no weight rule predicts position.
2946.prule: No positional rule is stated by any source. Stress is inherited Romance lexical stress whose position is contrastive within a right-edge window: after loss of every final unstressed vowel except -a, the dominant types are consonant-final oxytones (sumar, cavàl, gat) and -a-final paroxytones (cavala, amiga), but consonant-final paroxytones (diṣàstar, zàcul, epenthetic fóran, védar, sàbet), vowel-final oxytones (turnarà, murì, sustnù, piò) and, in Central Romagnol, sdrucciole (pìgura, scàtula) also occur, so the orthographic norms (Lapucci 1986, Vitali 2008, Ist. Schürr) mark the accent exactly where it departs from the dominant type. Ercolani's dictionary convention 'accent on the last syllable unless marked' encodes the same statistically dominant oxytone type, not a phonological rule. Michelotti: a prosodic constraint bans proparoxytones (syncope of all posttonic vowels, incl. -a-, in Central Romagnol; paragogic-vowel paroxytones in Sammarinese) and, in Sammarinese, heavy atonic word-final syllables.
2946.srule: No synchronic secondary-stress rule is stated. Michelotti 2008 mentions secondary stress only in his transcription key (ˌ = secondary stress, illustrated with Italian [ˈljɛviˌto]) and in a diachronic reconstruction of pre-syncope proparoxytones (descending ¹σ²σσ north of the Marecchia vs Tuscan-type ¹σσ²σ in the Pentapolis); his transcriptions of modern Sammarinese words carry a single stress mark ([tʃirˈvɛːl], [mɐɲɐˈrɔ]). The orthographic sources (Ercolani 1960, Lapucci 1986, Vitali 2008, Vitali & Pioggia 2010) say nothing about secondary stress.

2947.idn: The Supplement (pp. 79-108) is the defining source for Kitwa and says nothing about accent; the quoted 'Accent tonique' paragraph (p. 4) describes Kirundi at large (rund1242), which the author says all Warundi 'même les Watwa' speak, and his identity claim for Kitwa covers grammar…
2947.tone: Neither van der Burgt 1902 nor Ménard 1908 (Grammaire kirundi, par. 53-62 'De l'accent', pp. 20-24, held) mentions tone. Ménard's 'accent' for Kirundi proper is lexical: it distinguishes minimal pairs (kuràba 'regarder' / kuraba 'teindre'; kuhèra 'rémunérer' / kuhera 'finir'), is realised as vowel length/quality, monosyllabic radicals take no accent, disyllabic radicals are either unaccented or accented on the first syllable, polysyllables show several patterns -- no fixed position. Modern Kirundi (Meeussen 1959, not reached) is analysed as tonal with contrastive vowel length.

2948.prule: Two-register tone language (H/B). Non-verbal lexemes carry one of four lexical tone schemes (B, H, BH, HB; minimal pairs cited by the JALL notice). Verbs: a single melodic prominence ('la hauteur mélodique (ou accent)', an H) whose domain is the 'syntagme verbal' (person index + verb theme + mood marker); in the inaccompli it falls on the penult of that unit for lexical class I verbs (81,5 % of verb lexemes) and on the final for class II (18,5 %); in the accompli always on the final; under 'attraction tonale' from a preceding object/complement (not a subject) the H shifts one syllable leftward (final > penult, penult > antepenult) and pre-accentual syllables are levelled to the same register. No dynamic/intensity word stress is described anywhere.

2953.dq: Confronted with a language like Safwa, which permits only one prominent syllable per word ... In general, only one syllable per word can be prominent in a surface representation.
2953.prule: Culminative word prominence (one prominent syllable per word, phonetically higher pitch + greater intensity), analysed as a restricted tone system: each word carries one tonal specification [+/-TONE] on its final vowel. Non-verbal words: [-TONE] final -> antepenultimate prominence (APU, the unrestricted default; H assigned two morae before the final vowel, rules 9/11, mora-counting); [+TONE] final -> prominence on the ante-pre-stem-initial vowel (augment/emphatic/locative) if present, otherwise word-final (WF, rules 12-13); which pattern a stem takes is lexical ('should be marked in the lexicon'). Verbs: pattern fixed per tense (PU, APU, 4th mora, or a fixed morpheme). No weight-conditioned or syllable-count-fixed stress rule.
2953.srule: None: 'Safwa... permits only one prominent syllable per word' (p. 1); 'In general, only one syllable per word can be prominent in a surface representation' (p. 5). The only two-prominence form, the immediate-action tense (twaganabale), is analysed as two words joined by a reduced word boundary (pp. 5-6, fn. 6).

2953.tone: Voorhoeve deliberately uses 'prominence' as a cover term (fn. 2) and argues against the stress label: the single per-word prominence is derived from a [+/-TONE] mark on the word-final vowel by mora-counting rules, hence 'restricted tone system'; he derives it historically from an unrestricted Proto-Bantu tone system (sec. 8). Phonetically the prominent syllable has both higher pitch and greater intensity. Hyman 2006 (second-hand, in the copy consulted) calls it an obligatory one-H-mora-per-word system, 'cannot be SA' because mora-based; Philippson 1991 (second-hand, in the copy consulted) calls it 'langue accentuelle a melodie H*'. Position is lexical (nominal stems, two classes plus a closed PU class) or morphological (verb tense), never fixed by syllable count or weight.

tn.quote: For most Chorei speakers that I have worked with, there are no phonological tones. Only one elderly speaker (RB) demonstrated tonal distinctions in elicitation. ... the tonal distinctions produced by him were not recognised by the other consultants when I played his recordings back to them. ... I recorded these 9x2 = 18 items each from 3 speakers – NB, BH, NM – in the carrier phrase ... all the pairs were homophonous to all three consultants. ... Therefore, I concluded that for most Chorei speakers in Manikbond, there is no tonal phonology.

2955.tone: Two-level tone system (H/L): 'Er zijn geen regels aan te geven voor de tonen van den stam van een woord' / 'tons invariables mais imprévisibles'; rising word melodies are the most frequent; a slightly lower H before a pause is a pre-pausal/intonational realization, not a third toneme. De Witte says the high tone carries roughly the functional load stress has in European languages, while dynamic stress is weak, purely rhythmic, position unstated. Tylleskar 1987 (Lemvien-Nord variety; sec. 2.4 'Les tonèmes', pp. 104-108): 'La langue kisakata est une langue tonale', four tonemes (H, L, rising, falling) on CV radicals, H/L only elsewhere; absolute pitch depends on speaker and position in the phrase; no accent/stress section.

2958.heavy: The OPD Stress section speaks of 'heavy syllables' and 'light syllables' without defining them; its syllable-pattern table (p. 4) lists V, VV, CV, CVV, CVm as the surface types (kai.ka.la.si, yau.mai; lam.na, te.nem). Margetts 1999:10 defines the terms: 'The two vowels of a diphthong build a single heavy syllable (as do long vowels). Vowel length is not phonemic' and 'Syllables can have the pattern CV, CVV or CVN. In Saliba reduplication, two light syllables are reduplicated (CV) or one heavy syllable (CVV, CVN)'. So heavy = diphthongal CVV and nasal-closed CVN (the only coda); light = CV.
2958.dflt: penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word for verbs and for possessives used as nouns; for nouns with lexical roots of three or more light syllables, initial (~70%) or penultimate (~30%) with no rule stated
2958.prule: Default penultimate stress of the (suffixed) word, stated as a statistical tendency and conditioned by word class and syllable weight: verbs carry penultimate stress 'in at least 80% of the cases, but heavy syllables tend to attract the primary stress'; nouns whose lexical root has three or more light syllables take initial stress in about 70% of cases and penultimate in about 30%; possessives used as nouns take penultimate stress; determiners, adnominal possessives and subject-agreement prefixes are never stressed. Margetts 1999:11 states the simpler generalisation 'Primary stress lies generally on the penultimate syllable' with 'a few exceptions' (e.g. the name Saliba, initial stress) whose motivation is 'yet unclear'; Oetzel 2019:5 'Stress tends to be on the penultimate syllable... but there are exceptions'.
2958.srule: In unsuffixed lexical stems (nouns, verbs, adjectives), usually every second syllable preceding the primary stress carries secondary stress; reduplicants can carry secondary stress by the same pattern; suffixes shift the primary but not the secondary stress rightward, so up to three syllables may separate secondary and primary stress in inflected words (Oetzel & Oetzel 2004 OPD pp. 3-4). Margetts 1999:11 (earlier) and Oetzel 2019:5 (later, one line) state it more coarsely as secondary stress on the initial syllable (in words of more than two / more than four syllables).

There are different stress assignment constraints for verbs and nouns, and some of the other word classes are never stressed. 2959.dq: En sáliba, la palabra fonológica o grupo acentual puede estar constituido de dos a seis sílabas que llevan un acento fonético primario y están delimitadas por pausas que las preceden y las siguen. [...] Obviamente el tono se modifica bajo la influencia que la sintaxis ejerce sobre la palabra de la oración. (Benaissa 1979:90, 97)
2959.dloc: Benaissa 1979 sec. 1 'El grupo acentual' p. 90 and sec. 4 'Los fonemas suprasegmentales' pp. 96-97 (read); Morse & Frank 1997 sec. 2.1.2 'La sílaba, la palabra fonológica y el acento' pp. 30-31; Estrada Ramírez 2000 sec. 10.1.2 'El acento' p. 683.
2959.prule: One primary accent per phonological word (accent group of 2-6 syllables); its position is not predictable and can fall on any syllable of the word, so it is phonemic and contrastive (Benaissa: /wahamá/ 'huyeron' vs /wáhama/ '¿huyeron?', /núgu/ 'árboles' vs /nugúu/ 'árbol'; Estrada: /ˈdea/ 'carne' vs /deˈa/ 'blanco', /ˈcaha/ 'mi chinchorro' vs /caˈha/ 'mi boca', /ˈikʷe/ 'payarín' vs /iˈkʷe/ 'él come'). The accent is a pitch-cum-intensity-cum-length peak; word pitch is derived from it (high on the accented syllable, mid before, falling after).
2959.srule: Not mentioned in Benaissa 1979 (secs. 1 'El grupo acentual' p. 90, 4 'Los fonemas suprasegmentales' pp. 96-97, 5 'Ortografía' p. 98 read): the source describes one primary accent ('un acento fonético primario') per phonological word of 2-6 syllables and a single pitch peak; no secondary or rhythmic stress is discussed. 2959.exq_: No positional rule is stated ('El acento en sáliba no es predecible'). The one stated regularity is a correlate, not a placement rule: 'Todas las sílabas cuyo núcleo está formado por una serie idéntica de dos vocales son acentuadas y se caracterizan todas ellas además, por una ligera prolongación d…
2959.tone: Not a tone language. Benaissa 1979:96: 'El tono es predecible con base en el acento, coincidiendo el tono alto con la sílaba acentuada'; pre-accent syllables mid pitch, post-accent pitch falls to a markedly low final; sentence intonation and discourse level modify the word contour (p. 97). Morse & Frank 1997:30 repeat this ('El tono alto coincide con la sílaba acentuada'). The accent itself is described as a pitch-plus-intensity-plus-duration peak ('acento tonal... registro de tono ligeramente alto, así como una ligera intensidad sonora y duración del sonido nuclear', p. 90), i.e. stress-accent with pitch as its main cue, not lexical tone or accent classes.

2960.tone: OPD p. 3: 'There are two phonemic tones; high and low ' with the minimal pairs àrì/árí, èr/ér (acute/grave marks on the example words; the bracketed tone-mark glyphs after 'high' and 'low' are not legible in the PDF). Irwin 1974 sec. 0.4.3 (pp. 4-5): 'Two contrastive tones occur in Yui designated high... low' with the same pairs; 'Intonation overrides the tone patterns of individual words in sentences and so causes perturbation of the tonemes. Tone has been omitted in the writing of this grammar as it is deemed to be insignificant to the analysis.' OPD p. 4: 'phonemic tone is not written'. Tida 2011 (Japanese, sec. 2) treats the East Simbu group as word-tone languages and says Irwin 1974 noticed tone was distinctive in Yui but gave only two or three examples and no analysis; Tida gives no Yui stress data. So the language is a two-tone language in which the source ALSO states a fixed, non-phonemic word-final stress; coded fixed and quantity-insensitive with tone as the secondary rule. A verifier who holds that a stated lexical tone contrast should dominate would code tone or pitch accent with 'final non-phonemic stress'; the source text itself supports the fixed-final reading.
